Lorca la describió como un grito terrible que divide el paisaje en dos; Tía Anica la Piriñaca decía que cuando la cantaba a gusto la boca le sabía a sangre. La cantaban ya el Planeta (la de la Luna, la más antigua conocida) y el Fillo; luego Manuel Torre, Silverio, Paco la Luz, Cagancho, el Nitri, Curro Dulce, el Loco Mateo, el Mellizo, Terremoto de Jerez (que cantó toda la noche por siguiriyas con su madre muerta en brazos) y Juan Talega; hoy el Chocolate y José Menese. Antonio Mairena grabó unas cuarenta y cinco formas: es el siguiriyero más importante. Sus escuelas son Jerez y los Puertos, Cádiz y Triana. En el baile la difundió Vicente Escudero y Pilar López le añadió los palillos. La liviana, cante de campo, caminos y bandoleros, prepara la voz para la serrana, a la que Silverio dio brillo y con la que se remata por siguiriyas.

scenes.name: La caña, el polo y la petenera
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Tres cantes de la familia de la soleá. La caña, con ayes más arrastrados, se sitúa en la serranía de Ronda (un viajero inglés la oyó allí en 1830) o en la voz árabe gaunia, «canción»; la cantaron el Fillo, Tío José el Granaíno, Antonio Chacón, Pepe de la Matrona y Rafael Romero el Gallina, y hoy se usa más para el baile solemne. El polo se cantaba tras la caña, con la misma métrica; el de Tobalo, su supuesto creador, aparece ya en Estébanez Calderón y hoy se usa en la soleá apolá; Enrique Morente grabó el de Chacón. La petenera, melancólica y de origen incierto, se atribuye a una mujer de Paterna de la Ribera, «la perdición de los hombres», o a los sefardíes de los Balcanes; los gitanos la evitaron porque traía mala suerte. La cantaron la Niña de los Peines, Naranjito de Triana, Rafael Romero, Fosforito y hoy Pepe Menese.

scenes.name: Los cantes de Málaga: malagueñas, rondeñas, jaberas y verdiales
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Después de Sevilla y Cádiz, Málaga es la provincia con más variedad de cantes. La malagueña, cante libre, sin medida y sin baile, de rico toque, ha influido en las granaínas y en todos los cantes minero-levantinos. Nació en Álora (las malagueñas perotas) a partir de los fandangos abandolaos, acompañados de bandola; tras los anónimos y los de Cipriano Pitana, Francisco Jiménez y Joaquín Tabaco, Juan Breva le dio identidad propia, y Lorca escribió de su trino. Su esplendor es la segunda mitad del XIX, con el Canario, la Trini, Baldomero Pacheco y Fosforito el Viejo; también firmaron malagueñas el Mellizo, único gitano creador de una (inspirada en el prefacio de la misa), y Chacón. Diego Clavel recogió treinta y una en los noventa. La rondeña, de principios del XIX y de la tierra del Tobalo, es la pieza con que muchos guitarristas abren sus conciertos; la jabera, ruda y difícil, debe su nombre a una vendedora de habas y está casi perdida; los verdiales, de probable raíz morisca, apenas han cambiado y conservan la panda con violín, panderos, chinchines y cañas para la fiesta de san Juan.

scenes.name: Los tanguillos de Cádiz
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Vinculados al carnaval de Cádiz, son el soporte de chirigotas, coros y murgas; cantados en grupo pierden su naturaleza flamenca, que es individual, aunque como baile la conservan. Hay constancia de los «tangos graciosos» del barrio de La Viña en 1779, en la tonadilla La anónima de Tomás Abril, y el tango americano o de negros terminó de formarlos. Letras jocosas y satíricas: «el chiste ingenuo y feliz enfrente de la tragedia jonda del quejío» (Emilio Jiménez Díaz). Aurelio y Pericón de Cádiz, Manuel Vargas y la Perla los grabaron en la primera mitad del siglo XX, y hasta Mairena dejó dos. Chano Lobato, su mayor cultor, los elevó a cante noble y recrea la venta de los cuadros que popularizó Pericón.

scenes.name: Las tonás: martinetes, carceleras y deblas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Cantes sin acompañamiento, prueba de su antigüedad, en cuartetas octosílabas de intensa carga dramática y origen gitano indiscutible: son crónicas de la miseria, la cárcel y la persecución. Demófilo ya las daba en 1881 por «cantes viejos casi caídos en desuso»; en el siglo XIX hubo entre veintisiete y treinta y cuatro, cada una con el nombre de su creador. La más antigua es la de Tío Luis el de la Juliana, aguador y primer cantaor del que hay noticia (segunda mitad del siglo XVIII), conservada por Antonio Chacón y recreada por Pepe de la Matrona; se le atribuye también la toná de los pajaritos, que recuerda la tonada sefardí de los bilbilicos. Los martinetes toman el nombre del martillo de la fragua, aunque es difícil cantar mientras se forja: Tío Juane de Jerez montaba una fragua en escena en los setenta y ochenta, y Antonio el Bailarín creó su baile con martillo y yunque; la familia fragüera más antigua es la de los Cantorales de Cádiz, que Silverio visitaba. Las carceleras cantan la prisión y servían para pasar mensajes en romaní desde las rejas. La debla, único palo con nombre romaní («diosa»), es religiosa, casi perdida y muy difícil; llegó a hoy por Tomás Pavón en los cuarenta y la recuperó Antonio Mairena.

scenes.name: Las sevillanas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Nacen de las seguidillas castellanas, que en Sevilla se hicieron más vivas y fáciles de repetir: cuatro coplas para bailar en pareja un galanteo, con temas andaluces, amorosos o rocieros (corraleras, rocieras, bíblicas, de feria, marineras, romeras). Lorca recogió una del siglo XVIII. Su gran auge comercial llegó en los setenta, con millones de discos que daban envidia a los flamencos; las han grabado con jondura Manuel Vallejo, la Niña de los Peines, la Paquera de Jerez, el Turronero, Chiquetete y Camarón.

scenes.name: El fandango
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Muy apreciado por su musicalidad y fácil de interpretar, no es un palo básico pero no es menor: la vieja división entre cantes grandes y chicos está obsoleta, y la jondura la pone el intérprete, no la antigüedad del palo. Canto para bailar de origen muy antiguo e incierto (Corominas lo deriva del portugués fado; hay quien le ve un lejano origen árabe), aparece por escrito en un entremés de 1705 y lo describe el deán Manuel Martí en 1712; en el siglo XIX fue el cante y baile nacional español, y a finales de siglo se aflamencó en Andalucía y dejó de bailarse. De él salen las granaínas, las malagueñas y los cantes de Levante, y hay fandangos propios en Lucena, Cabra, Puente Genil, Jaén, Granada o Almería. Su apogeo en la ópera flamenca lo desprestigió tanto que a cantaores como Pepe Menese les parece un insulto que se lo pidan; desde los años ochenta se revaloriza.

facts.body: Rock fans in 1979 were divided over The Knack's "My Sharona," loving it for its success but loathing it for scoring "Rock's first big number one in a year full of disco" and for its "faux Beatles imagery and sexist lyrics." "Arguably the Nickelback of their day, the NAC were both loved and loathed by Rock fans in 1979."

facts.title: Opening for Toto (January 26, 1979)
facts.body: In a misguided attempt by major record labels to market punk, The Ramones were chosen to open shows for Toto. This unusual pairing occurred on one tour, including a date in Lake Charles, Louisiana, on January 26, 1979, where they also shared the bill with Foreigner and Blue Oyster Cult. "the Ramones were picked to open shows for Toto."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 8
facts.name: The Ramones

facts.title: Attempted Crossover with "Rock 'n' Roll High School" (1979)
facts.body: In 1979, The Ramones appeared in the B-movie *Rock 'n' Roll High School*, produced by Roger Corman. The film capitalized on the late 70s musical movie craze and starred P.J. Soles as Riff Randall. The Ramones, though not the first choice (Cheap Trick and Todd Rundgren were considered), provided a "very punchy theme song" and looked the part of youth rebels. The movie was a critical success and modest box office earner, intended as a mainstream crossover vehicle for the band into the 1980s. "A claimed by critics and a modest box office success upon its release in 1979, Rock and Roll High School should have been the ticket for the Ramones too at last make a mainstream crossover into the 1980s."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: This Ain’t No Party! Edition Part 2
facts.name: The Ramones

facts.title: Emergence of Distinct Musical Bases (1979-1983)
facts.body: The distinct musical bases that define hip hop culture emerged from a rapid evolution of rap between 1979 and 1983. Prior to this, early rap releases, despite being foundational, were still rooted in funk, boogie, and late disco, rather than the later characteristic sounds of hip hop. "no recuerda todavía esas bases que de lo que luego sería el hip hop."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: El RAP antes del RAP (los primeros años del rap)
facts.name: hip hop

facts.title: Origin as Recorded Medium (1979)
facts.body: Rap had existed for over a decade since DJ Kool Herc's 1973 party, but it became a recorded medium with the release of "Rapper's Delight" in 1979. This marked a crucial step in its journey towards mainstream pop recognition. "rap had been a recorded medium for more than four years since 1979's rappers delight."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: What’s 1984 Got to Do with It Edition Part 1
facts.name: hip hop

facts.title: Sylvia Robinson's Pivotal Role (1979)
facts.body: Sylvia Robinson (formerly Little Sylvia and Mickey & Sylvia) played a foundational role in the commercialization of hip-hop in 1979. With financing from her husband Joe Robinson's gangster friend Morris Levy, she was instrumental in recognizing and capitalizing on the genre's commercial potential. "Because Sylvia Robinson, who had been little Sylvia, and the woman calling her lover boy, became to hip-hop, what Sam Phillips was to rock and roll."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Malcolm McLaren's Early Advocacy (Late 1979)
facts.body: Starting in late 1979, art-oriented members of the British punk community, notably former Sex Pistols manager Malcolm McLaren, attempted to popularize the phrase "New Wave." McLaren sought to use this term to describe the musical landscape in the months following the Sex Pistols' breakup. "The art C1s amongst the British punk community, including ex-sextal manager Malcolm McLaren, tried to get people to accept this word, this phrase beginning in late 1979, as Malcolm sought to describe his world in the months after the sex pistols broke out."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Etymology: Part 1
facts.name: New Wave

facts.title: Era (1979-1985)
facts.body: The New Wave era began in 1979 and maintained a strong presence until at least 1985. It transitioned from an underground sound connected to punk rock to becoming a very mainstream genre, defining the mainstream for a period. "The New Wave era started in 1979 and had a good run before it was done by, oh at least 1985."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 8
facts.name: New Wave

facts.title: Emergence (1979)
facts.body: In 1979, concurrent with the ongoing Post-Punk scene, New Wave music was emerging. This period was characterized by a rapid birth and diversification of musical styles. "en 1979, estaban naciendo la vez el new wave."

facts.title: US Breakthrough Summer (1979)
facts.body: The summer of 1979 was the definitive "breakthrough summer of New Wave" in America, marked by power pop bands like Cheap Trick, The Knack, and The Cars achieving their highest-charting hits. "In America, that was the breakthrough summer of New Wave, as power pop bands like Cheap Trick."

facts.title: Sid Vicious Ashes Allegedly Spilled at Heathrow Terminal 4 (February 1979)
facts.body: After Sid Vicious's death on February 2, 1979 (heroin overdose while awaiting trial for the murder of Nancy Spungen), his mother Anne Beverly had him cremated. Two weeks later, allegedly drunk while returning to London through Heathrow Airport, she tripped, fell, and spilled Sid's ashes in the terminal — some reportedly embedded in the carpet and sucked into the ventilation system. Rumor holds that Sid Dust still circulates through Terminal 4. However, those with knowledge say this is not what happened: what is confirmed is that before returning to England, Anne took his ashes to Nancy Spungen's grave in Philadelphia and spread them there. What is also confirmed is that New York police tipped off London police, who raided Anne's Notting Hill home, found drugs, and arrested her. Anne Beverly died on September 6, 1996, after carefully putting her affairs in order and then consuming a large quantity of painkillers, tranquilizers, and alcohol. "Rumor has it that Sid Dust still circulates throughout terminal four."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 100 weirdest Things in Alt-Rock: Part 10
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Heroin Overdose (April 2, 1979)
facts.body: Sid Vicious died of a heroin overdose in his new girlfriend's apartment on April 2, 1979, officially closing the case on Nancy Spungen's murder with Sid as the culprit, though questions still linger. "He died of a heroin overdose in his new girlfriend's apartment on April 2, 1979, so officially, Sid killed Nancy."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Steven Morris - Yorkshire Ripper Suspect (1979)
facts.body: Drummer Steven Morris was briefly a suspect in the case of the Yorkshire Ripper, an English serial killer responsible for at least 13 murders. Police noticed a correlation between the murder locations and the stops on a 1979 Joy Division tour, leading them to suspect Steven. He was later cleared, and Peter Sutcliffe was arrested for the crimes. "Steven was briefly a suspect in the case of the Yorkshire Ripper, an English serial killer who murdered at least 13 women. Police noticed that the location of the murders mirrored that of a 1979 Joy Division tour and thought that Steven might be their guy."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Couples in Music
facts.name: Joy Division

facts.title: Ian Curtis's Epilepsy Diagnosis (January 23, 1979)
facts.body: Ian Curtis began experiencing seizures in the fall of 1978, which rapidly became frequent. On January 23, 1979, his diagnosis of epilepsy was confirmed, described as a grim and severe case, with a doctor warning that his life would be dominated by the disease unless he adhered to a regimen of strong medication. "Ian started having seizures in the fall of 1978. They quickly became frequent. On January 23rd, 1979, the diagnosis was confirmed. And the diagnosis was grim. His case was really bad."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Musicians Battling Disease Part 1
facts.name: Joy Division

facts.title: BBC Live Recording (November 26, 1979)
facts.body: Joy Division recorded a live session for DJ John Peel at the BBC on November 26, 1979. This recording, along with many others by British bands, was facilitated and even mandated by the "Needle Time" provisions, which required the BBC to produce its own live music content. "Joy Division recorded live at the BBC for DJ John Peel on November 26, 1979. And thanks to the Needle Time provisions that were in place for all of British radio until 1988, an unbelievable amount of history was captured."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Useless information
facts.name: Joy Division

facts.body: The recording of Joy Division's first album commenced in March or April of 1979. "a primeros en 1979, marzo abril en 1979 comenzaba la grabación del primer álbum de Yoid y Division"

facts.body: Despite the short time span, Joy Division underwent a profound evolution between 1979 and early 1980, resulting in a significantly different sound and approach by the latter period. facts.title: Hepatitis from Gobbing – 1979, Spat in Mouth During Performance
facts.body: In the early British punk scene, audience members competed to spit at bands on stage as a sign of enthusiasm following a newspaper article depicting the practice. During a 1979 Clash performance, Joe Strummer was singing with his mouth open when an audience member's spit landed directly in it. The result was a significant case of hepatitis. The practice of spitting at performers, known as "gobbing," was common enough that performers were routinely covered in phlegm and mucus during shows. "Joe Strummer was singing. His mouth was open and the result was a really nasty case of hepatitis."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 100 Weirdest Things in Alt-Rock: Part 4
facts.name: The Clash

facts.title: Paul Simonon's Bass Trashing Incident (1979)
facts.body: During a show at the Palladium in New York on September 21, 1979, bassist Paul Simonon smashed his instrument on stage. His frustration stemmed from the crowd's perceived lack of engagement, which he attributed to bouncers preventing the audience from standing up. The incident occurred around 10:43 pm, as evidenced by his broken wristwatch. This moment was captured in an iconic, out-of-focus photograph by Penny Smith, which later became the cover of "London Calling." "Simmon was in a very bad mood that night at the palladium in New York. He was upset that the crowd just wasn't into the gig, largely because the bouncers had refused to let the audience stand up and get into the show."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Digital Debris Part 2: Album Artwork
facts.name: The Clash

facts.title: Emergence in Early 1979
facts.body: By early 1979, the original punk rock scene had largely dissipated, giving way to the era of post-punk, a period characterized by a rapid succession of new sounds and attitudes that could only have evolved in the wake of punk's initial emergence. "By early 1979, the original punk rock scene had pretty much burned itself out. And we entered the era of post punk, a time when it seemed like a new sound attitude came out every day."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?
facts.name: Post-Punk

facts.title: Late Disco Influence on Early Rap (1979)
facts.body: Late disco music contributed significantly to the background sound of the first modern rap releases in 1979, alongside funk and boogie, before hip hop developed its own distinct musical identity. "recuerdan sobre todo al buggy y no tanto al hip hop hay un es como que entre el rap como una evolución dentro de lo que sería la música fankey de lo que sería el buggy del final de la música disco."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: El RAP antes del RAP (los primeros años del rap)
facts.name: Disco

facts.title: Transition from Rap (1979-1983)
facts.body: Rap underwent a rapid evolution between 1979 and 1983, during which it separated itself from its late disco roots to establish the distinct musical foundations of hip hop. "acabaría separando el rap con esos restos era música buggy y era música disco tardía a lo que sería lo que serían las bases del hip hop."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: El RAP antes del RAP (los primeros años del rap)
facts.name: Disco

facts.title: Anti-Disco Riots (1979)
facts.body: In 1979, the anti-disco riots erupted in the United States, marking a significant downturn for the disco movement. Conservative groups publicly burned disco albums, leading to widespread censorship in many conservative regions. These events ultimately signaled the beginning of the end for disco and curtailed the careers of many prominent artists in the genre. "justo en 1979 se generan los estúrbios antidiscos cuando grupos conservadores empiezan a quemar públicamente álbumes de música disco y empieza a ver a una censura enorme en muchas partes son tanto conservadoras de Estados Unidos."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Grace Jones - Inicios de la Disco Queen
facts.name: Disco

facts.title: Death by Heroin Overdose (1979)
facts.body: Approximately 13 months after the Sex Pistols' final concert in San Francisco on January 14, 1978, Sid Vicious tragically died from a heroin overdose. This event marked the definitive end of his brief and tumultuous career with the band. "And it was the last time we'd see them with Sid Vicious because 13 months later, he'd be dead of a heroin overdose."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5
facts.name: Sid Vicious

facts.title: Murder Charge and Bail (1979)
facts.body: Sid Vicious was charged with Nancy Spungen's murder, with his trial scheduled for February 2, 1979. He was released from jail on $50,000 bail prior to the trial.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9
facts.name: Sid Vicious

facts.title: Fatal Overdose (1979)
facts.body: The night before his trial, on February 1, 1979, Sid attended a party in his honor at his new girlfriend Michelle Robinson's home, with his mother and friends present. His mother supplied him with heroin, and later he took more from her purse. He overdosed and was put to bed around 3 AM. No doctor was called to avoid violating his bail conditions. The next morning, he was found dead, naked, on top of the covers.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9
facts.name: Sid Vicious

facts.title: Release from Jail and New Girlfriend – February 1, 1979
facts.body: After 55 days in jail, Sid was released on bail on February 1, 1979, having completely detoxed. While incarcerated, he had managed to find a new girlfriend, Michelle Robinson. "After 55 days in jail, Sid is out on bail and by this time he is completely detoxed."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Sid Vicious
facts.name: Sid Vicious

facts.title: Fatal Heroin Overdose – February 2, 1979
facts.body: To celebrate his freedom, Sid's mother arranged for a drug dealer, Peter Kodak, to deliver heroin to Michelle Robinson's apartment after a spaghetti dinner. Sid took a "taste" of 99% pure heroin. Being fully detoxed, his body was super vulnerable, and he overdosed, dying in his sleep as his heart rate slowed and lungs filled with fluid. "Apparently, the heroine he took the night before was 99% pure."

facts.title: Columbus Holiday Inn Bar Fight (March 10, 1979) – Racist Remarks, Punch from Bonnie Bramlett, Career Nearly Ruined in America
facts.body: On March 10, 1979, Elvis Costello and his entourage were drinking heavily in a bar at a Holiday Inn in Columbus, Ohio, when they encountered Stephen Stills's party. Costello made blatant racist remarks about Ray Charles and James Brown. Stephen Stills's companion Bonnie Bramlett punched Costello, a full brawl broke out, and the incident made national news. American media sided with Stills; Costello became toxic and his American career took years to recover. He later described the incident in his memoirs *Unfaithful Music and Disappearing Ink* (2015) and acknowledged it without denial or excuse. "An old barfight from 37 years ago — but there are real serious things that haven't been fixed that are not my doing or my responsibility."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 10 Terrible Career Moves
facts.name: Elvis Costello

facts.title: Columbus, Ohio Incident (1979)
facts.body: In the spring of 1979, during a drunken exchange at a hotel bar in Columbus, Ohio, Costello used racial slurs to insult several African American musical artists, including James Brown and Ray Charles, in front of members of Stephen Stills' band. When details of this incident were leaked to the press, his American reputation was tarnished, leading radio stations to pull the *Armed Forces* LP from rotation and causing later dates on his US tour to sell poorly. Costello, who had previously been involved in England's Rock Against Racism movement, felt foolish and expressed deep regret for the incident in later interviews, stating in 1982, "what could I do, hold up a sign that read, I really like black people?" "After Word got around that spring of an incident at a hotel bar in Columbus, Ohio between Costello and members of Stephen Stills band."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

facts.title: Compact Disk Development Partnership (1979)
facts.body: Sony joined Phillips in 1979 to collaborate on the development of the compact disk technology. Their involvement was instrumental in setting a worldwide standard for CDs, including specifications for material (polycarbonate), diameter (120 millimeters), laser reading direction (inside-out), and maximum length (74 minutes), reputedly to accommodate the Sony chairman's favorite Beethoven symphony. "In 1979 Sony gets on board to help out with development."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 8
facts.name: Sony Music

facts.title: Collaboration with Philips on CD Standards (1979)
facts.body: Sony teamed up with Philips in 1979 after both companies realized they were working toward the same goal for a new music storage format. This collaboration involved splitting research costs, sharing knowledge, and establishing the proper standards, resulting in the "Red Book CDDA standard." "In 1979, when Sony and Phillips realized that they were working towards the same goal, the companies teamed up to split the costs of research, to share knowledge, and to come up with all the proper standards for making this new music storage format."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Rise and Fall of the CD
facts.name: Sony Music

facts.title: Contribution to Red Book CDDA Standard (1979)
facts.body: Sony, having a head start in digital storage technology, contributed its expertise to the creation of the Red Book CDDA standard. This collection of specifications, designed in 1979, remains the basis for manufacturing compact discs globally today. "Meanwhile, Sony, which had a head start in digital storage technology, contributed what they knew. The result was something known as the Red Book CDDA standard, which is a collection of specifications that are still used to make compact discs everywhere on the planet today."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Rise and Fall of the CD
facts.name: Sony Music

facts.title: CD Development Collaboration (1979)
facts.body: Sony, having a head start in digital storage technology, teamed up with Philips in 1979 to develop the compact disk. Sony contributed all its knowledge from prior work, including demonstrations of optical disks in 1977 and 1978 that could hold varying lengths of music. The collaboration shared research costs and aimed to establish proper standards for the new music storage format. `"Meanwhile, Sony, which had a head start in digital storage technology, contributed everything that they knew."`

facts.title: Walkman (1979) - Portable Cassette Player
facts.body: Sony launched the Walkman on July 1, 1979, as a modification of their "Pressman" audio recorder for journalists. Requested by Sony head Masaru Ibuka for long flights, the original TPS-LP2 model was small, light, and came with high-quality headphones. It uniquely featured two headphone jacks, reflecting an initial belief that users wouldn't want complete isolation. Initially branded as Soundabout, Stowaway, or Freestyle in various regions, it was eventually standardized globally as the Walkman. Priced at $150 in 1979 (nearly $600 today), Sony projected monthly sales of 5,000 units but sold 30,000 in its first 60 days, fundamentally changing portable music and boosting cassette sales. `"So imagine his surprise. When on July 1st, 1979, Sony started selling something called the Walkman."`
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 1
facts.name: Sony Music

facts.title: Introduction of the Walkman (1979)
facts.body: In 1979, Sony began selling the Walkman, a portable cassette player designed to be worn on a belt and used with headphones. This product quickly became a commercial success but also ignited a patent dispute with Andreas Pavel, who had conceived a similar device years earlier. "It was 1979. Sony started selling something called the Walkman."

facts.title: Introduction of the Walkman (1979)
facts.body: In 1979, Sony revolutionized the music industry with the introduction of the Walkman, the first truly portable device designed for listening to cassette tapes. This invention fundamentally transformed music consumption by enabling personal, on-the-go audio experiences, marking a pivotal moment in musical culture. "el grandísimo invento que cambiaría la cultura musical para siempre fue cuando en 1979 Sony presenta el Waltman, el primera para toportátil para escuchar casets."

"Meanwhile, Sony, which had a head start in digital storage technology, contributed what they knew. The result was something known as the Red Book CDDA standard, which is a collection of specifications that are still used to make compact discs everywhere on the planet today."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Rise and Fall of the CD
facts.name: Sony Music

facts.title: Introduction of the Walkman (1979)
facts.body: In 1979, Sony began selling the Walkman, a portable cassette player designed to be worn on a belt and used with headphones. This product quickly became a commercial success but also ignited a patent dispute with Andreas Pavel, who had conceived a similar device years earlier. "It was 1979. Sony started selling something called the Walkman."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Inventors
facts.name: Sony Music

facts.title: Walkman (1979) - Portable Cassette Player
facts.body: Sony launched the Walkman on July 1, 1979, as a modification of their "Pressman" audio recorder for journalists. Requested by Sony head Masaru Ibuka for long flights, the original TPS-LP2 model was small, light, and came with high-quality headphones. It uniquely featured two headphone jacks, reflecting an initial belief that users wouldn't want complete isolation. Initially branded as Soundabout, Stowaway, or Freestyle in various regions, it was eventually standardized globally as the Walkman. Priced at $150 in 1979 (nearly $600 today), Sony projected monthly sales of 5,000 units but sold 30,000 in its first 60 days, fundamentally changing portable music and boosting cassette sales. `"So imagine his surprise. When on July 1st, 1979, Sony started selling something called the Walkman."`
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 1
facts.name: Sony Music

facts.title: Early CD Technology Showcases (1979-1982)
facts.body: Classical music played a pivotal role in the early demonstration and commercialization of compact disc technology. The first test pressing in 1979 featured the Berlin Philharmonic performing Richard Strauss's "An Alpine Symphony," selected for its clarity and dynamic range. Later, Chopin's waltzes, performed by Claudia Arrau, became the first CD produced for public consumption on August 17, 1982. "The first test pressing, a CD used to demonstrate the new technology, was a recording of the Berlin Philharmonic, conducted by Herbert von Karrihan, performing Richard Strauss' and Elpine Symphony. This appeared in 1979, and this recording was chosen for its clarity and wide range of dynamics, something that the compact is promised."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Rise and Fall of the CD
facts.name: classical

facts.title: Cincinnati Concert Tragedy (1979)
facts.body: On December 3, 1979, almost exactly ten years after the Elton Mont incident, 11 people were trampled to death at a Who concert in Cincinnati. The fatalities occurred as fans stampeded for prime spots in a general admission area. This tragedy led to significant changes in concert safety rules globally, including limiting ticket sales based on venue square footage and implementing new guidelines for ushers, security personnel, and evacuation plans. "After this tragedy, a number of new rules were enacted around the world."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Fans and Fatalities
facts.name: The Who

facts.title: Cincinnati Concert Stampede (December 3, 1979)
facts.body: On December 3, 1979, a stampede occurred outside a sold-out Who concert at Riverfront Coliseum in Cincinnati, which had sold 18,348 tickets. A large crowd, many with general admission tickets, pushed forward after hearing music, believing The Who had started early. Only two doors were initially open, and the intense crush over 40 minutes led to 11 deaths by asphyxiation and 26 injuries, mostly among teenagers and young adults. "whenever you go through the stories of rock disasters, you always end up what happened at a who concert in Cincinnati on December 3, 1979."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Rock's Greatest Disasters
facts.name: The Who

facts.title: Riverfront Colosseum Tragedy (December 3, 1979)
facts.body: At a Who concert on December 3, 1979, 11 fans were tragically crushed to death while waiting to enter the Riverfront Colosseum in Cincinnati. This general admission "Festival Seating" arrangement had already raised safety concerns. "On December 3rd, 1979, 11 fans of the who were killed when they were crushed to death while waiting to enter the Riverfront Colosseum in Cincinnati to see a concert."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 58 - WKRP in Cincinnati
facts.name: The Who

facts.title: Early Retirement from Touring (1979)
facts.body: Kate Bush famously retired from extensive touring in 1979 at the age of 20, after releasing only two albums. Her decision was influenced by the exhausting nature of touring and, significantly, by the tragic death of her lighting director in a fall during a warm-up show for "The Tour of Life." "First, she found the whole ordeal exhausting. Second, during a warm-up show for that road trip, which was called The Tour of Life, her lighting director was killed in a fall. And that really soured things."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 1: (100-91)
facts.name: Kate Bush

facts.title: Two-Tone Records Founded 1979 – Black-and-White Logo Based on Peter Tosh Photo; Anti-Racist Mission
facts.body: Jerry Dammers founded Two-Tone Records, naming it after the black-and-white suits worn by mods and skinheads of the 1960s and after the peaceful multiracial makeup of the band. The label's logo — a man in a black and white suit, white shirt, black tie, sunglasses, pork pie hat, white socks, and black loafers — was drawn by Dammers based on a photo of Peter Tosh when he was a member of the Wailers. The character was named Walt Jabsco (Walt after Walt Disney). Two-Tone had an explicit anti-racism message at a time when racial tensions in the UK were getting out of control. "Two-tone became the core of the second wave of Scott."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: A Not-So Brief History of Ska: Part 1
facts.name: The Specials

"For example, in 1979, Singer Jello Biafra ran for mayor of San Francisco."

facts.title: "Queen of Gay Discos" and Anti-Disco Backlash (1979)
facts.body: At the peak of her success in 1979, coinciding with the release of a work described as "Queen of Gay Discos," Grace Jones's popularity was negatively impacted by the anti-disco riots. During this period, conservative groups publicly burned disco albums, leading to widespread censorship in many conservative parts of the United States. "cuando saca el mío y de Queen of Gay Discos pues lamentablemente bien el problema porque justo en 1979 se generan los estúrbios antidiscos."

facts.title: Reinvention After Anti-Disco Riots (1979)
facts.body: While the anti-disco riots of 1979 signaled the end for many disco artists, for Grace Jones, it was merely another step in her career and a crucial moment for reinterpretation, ultimately propelling her to even greater heights. She is characterized as a figure of constant reinvention, relentless provocation, and always pushing boundaries. "para grillos no solo fue un paso más en su carrera sino que fue el momento de una reinterpretación que la gría incluso volver todavía más alto porque ella es un personaje de reinvención constante de provocación constante y de siempre ir más allá."

facts.title: Recording Anecdote
facts.body: In the summer of 1979, The Clash entered the studio to record this album with producer Guy Stevens. During a warm-up session where the band covered an old blues song by American singer Vince Taylor, Stevens secretly hit record. Despite the band's concerns that their performance was sloppy and the tempo was wrong, Stevens accepted the take, asserting that "all rock and roll speeds up." The resulting energy, as heard in tracks like "Brand New Cadillac," contrasts with modern, digitally corrected recordings. "The clash was bewildered. We can't use that. It was sloppy. The tempo was all wrong. We listened to how we speed up through the song."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 10 Things That Really Annoy Me

facts.body: Released just before Christmas 1979, the album features iconic artwork. The cover photo, an out-of-focus shot taken by Penny Smith on September 21, 1979, at the Palladium in New York, depicts bassist Paul Simonon trashing his instrument. Simonon was in a bad mood that night because bouncers prevented the audience from standing up and engaging with the show, leading him to destroy his bass near the end of the set. The exact time, 10:43 pm, is known because Paul broke his wristwatch while smashing his bass. The photo was accidentally taken by Smith, who was startled and didn't have time to change her Pentax camera lens. Initially embarrassed by the shot's quality, Penny was convinced by Joe Strummer the next day that he loved it and it should be the cover. The artwork's layout and typography were partly inspired by Elvis Presley's self-titled 1956 album. It has since been named the best rock and roll photo of all time and became an official British postage stamp. "At first, Penny was really embarrassed at the quality of the shot. But the next day, Joe Strummer said he loved it and that it should be the cover of the next Clash album."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.body: Released on December 14, 1979, "London Calling" is a powerful double album that came after The Clash's North American tour, where they gathered new ideas and recognized the end of the punk era. The band integrated diverse genres like reggae, dub, rockabilly, calypso, garage rock, rap, and even disco, fueled by anger towards their management, record label, lawsuits, and Britain's "Winter of Discontent." Twelve of its nineteen songs were completed in just three days in August 1979. Rolling Stone named it the best album of the 1980s, solidifying its place as one of the greatest and most influential rock and roll albums of all time. "The final result was what Rolling Stone named as the best album of the 1980s. A powerful, powerful double album entitled London Calling."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.body: This double album, released on December 14, 1979, featured 19 songs and marked the band's creative peak, becoming one of the most influential records ever and assuring The Clash's reputation. It expanded their sound to include Ska, Reggae, Calypso, Disco, Garage Rock, Rockabilly, and Rap, with some songs inspired by a North American tour and others by the music in the streets of Pimlico, London. Recorded over just a few days in August 1979, including 12 songs bashed out in three days, the album, originally titled "The New Testament," was produced by Guy Stevens, who prioritized feel over technical perfection. The band demanded its release as a double album, but to make it affordable for their fans, they agreed to package it like a single, lower the price, and accept a lower royalty rate.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.body: This third album marked a significant evolution from the band's earlier fierce punk rock, incorporating diverse influences like reggae, dub, ska, blues, R&B, soul, and rockabilly. It demonstrated their readiness to discard old punk dogmas and inject new ideas to enhance their messages on racism, drug abuse, corrupt police, and unemployment, becoming known as one of the greatest rock records of all time. "The result was a third album that was unlike anything anyone could have ever expected out of that old punk rock stew. Record was called London Calling."

The cover has become immensely popular, launching a million t-shirts, posters, and imitations, including a Disney co-opted Mickey Mouse t-shirt in 2012. facts.title: Debut Album
facts.body: The recording of Joy Division's first album, *Unknown Pleasures*, began in 1979. It is considered a possible peak work of Post-Punk and a key origin point for the genre. The pure recording process was very fast, taking only three to five weekends, but the overall production was protracted because the band members had day jobs and could only record on Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays. The band entered the recording sessions with a clear idea and polished vision for the songs, having already developed a detailed demo and experienced a failed recording contract with RCA. The album was released several months after its recording. It achieved relative success, selling well for an independent, almost self-produced album, though it was not a major chart hit and didn't reach the top 70s. Its success enabled the band to tour extensively and become full-time professional musicians. Despite its current critical acclaim, *Unknown Pleasures* was not widely reviewed at the time of its release, and many contemporary "reviews" found today are retrospective, often from the late 1990s or 2000s. The album's legacy is that it significantly influenced many bands, like The Cure, who in turn influenced the public, rather than directly influencing the general public itself, drawing a comparison to The Velvet Underground's debut. "Continuamos este pequeño especial sobre la vida y la carrera de J-Division en el punto en el que lo habíamos dejado el momento anterior, que es justo 1979 cuando comienza la grabación de No Pleasure's, el primer disco del J-Division."

facts.body: The Knack was among the power pop bands that achieved their biggest hits during the summer of 1979, which was recognized as the breakthrough summer for New Wave in America. "as power pop bands like Cheap Trick. The neck, and the cars. All scored their biggest hits to date."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Angry Young Men Edition Part 1
facts.name: The Knack

facts.title: Nuke the Knack T-shirts (1979)
facts.body: In 1979, discerning rock fans expressed their disdain for The Knack by wearing "Nuke the NAC t-shirts" due to the band's faux Beatles imagery, sexist lyrics, and the song's chart success in a disco-heavy year. "Descerning Rock fans even wore Nuke the NAC t-shirts that year."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Hits of the Year Edition Part 2
facts.name: The Knack

facts.title: Shared Tour with The Ramones (January 26, 1979)
facts.body: In a bizarre pairing reflecting major labels' misunderstanding of punk, The Ramones were chosen to open shows for Toto on a tour. A notable instance occurred on January 26, 1979, in Lake Charles, Louisiana, where the bill also included Foreigner and Blue Oyster Cult. "the Ramones were picked to open shows for Toto."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 8

facts.body: Pink Floyd enlisted Bob Ezrin to help sort out a project they were struggling with in the late 1970s, resulting in "The Wall," which became one of the biggest selling records of all time. "And when Pink Floyd got hopelessly bogged down with a project in the late 1970s, they called in Bob Ezra and disordered out. And the results? Just one of the biggest sawing records of all time, The Wall."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.body: Richie Edwards of the Manic Street Preachers developed an intense identification with the character of Pink, the "burned out rock star" subject of Pink Floyd's iconic album *The Wall*, during a period of his severe mental decline. "He began to identify with the character of Pink, the burned out rock star subject of Pink Floyd's The Wall."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 9: The Disappearance of Richey Edwards
facts.name: The Wall

facts.body: The concept for this album began to form in Roger Waters' mind in 1977, driven by his frustration with performing in large stadiums where audiences seemed more interested in beer than the music. He proposed the idea to the rest of Pink Floyd in 1978. The album served as the basis for the 1980 tour, during which a massive brick wall was gradually constructed on stage throughout the first half of the show, symbolizing the "growing isolation" felt by the burned-out rock star protagonist, Pink. "The wall was born out of the frustration that Roger Waters felt about performing in large stadiums. He started thinking about it in 1977 and proposed it to the rest of Pink Floyd in 1978."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 42 - Rock Operas of the 70s

facts.title: Second with Brian Eno
facts.body: This was the band's third album overall, and their second collaboration with producer Brian Eno. It marked a significant evolution in their sound, becoming incredibly danceable and fresh due to its strong, funky rhythm section. "By their third album, their second with producer Brian Eno, they devolved into something so dancing, yet so fresh, that you couldn't help moving to the beat."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 7: All the rest
